newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: NSW Australia crops are in but rain needed - farmers.
newsitem.headline: NSW Australia crops are in but rain needed - farmers.

text.p: Patchy rain over the last month in Australia's New South Wales (NSW) wheat belt had allowed more areas to plant crops, the NSW Farmers Association said.
But more rain was needed in the central and southern wheat belt in the next two weeks to generate growth, senior vice president John Cobb said in a statement.

"If we can get the bare minimum rainfall needed every month for the next four months there could be a chance of harvesting a crop that will earn about A$2 billion for the NSW (state) economy, even though El Nino is threatening," he said.

A current El Nino effect, a weather condition based on South Pacific sea surface temperatures and their interaction with the atmosphere, has prompted weather bureau predictions that Australia faces a winter/spring drought.
If rain did not come, farmers who had been forced to borrow from the bank to get the thousands of dollars needed to finance the crop would face ruin, Cobb said.
Few areas of NSW had had sufficient rain to build up soil moisture to promote growth for most of the growing period of the crop, he said.
"In many areas, crops have been planted on light falls, because crops planted after early June are less likely to have the high protein content which makes wheat more valuable," he said.
"If no follow-up rain comes, the crop will die and the farmers will lose their investment," he said.
Lack of rain had resulted in 45 percent of NSW being declared by the state government to be in drought, he said.

"Dams are running dry and even if rain fell now, the warm days needed to promote pasture growth are unlikely before October. I expect that the government will soon announce that more than half of the state is in drought," Cobb said.
